## Part-Time Employee vs Contractor for a Melbourne Bakery

For a bakery needing **20 hours/week for 6 months**, the choice usually comes down to **control and consistency** versus **flexibility and lower admin**. For a hands-on retail/food role with fixed shifts, a **part-time employee** is often the safer operational fit; a contractor can work well only if the work is genuinely independent and outcome-based.

## Side-by-Side Comparison

| Factor | Part-Time Employee | Contractor |
|---|---|---|
| Control | You can set shifts, tasks, standards, and supervision | More limited control; contractor should decide how the work is done |
| Scheduling flexibility | Good for regular rosters, but less flexible for last-minute changes | High flexibility if work is project-based or irregular |
| Training time | Usually more upfront training, then smoother day-to-day consistency | Less training if they arrive already skilled; still need onboarding to your processes |
| Payroll/admin burden | Higher: payroll, super, leave, records, tax withholding, compliance | Lower if truly a contractor: invoices instead of payroll, usually less ongoing admin |
| Risk considerations | Lower misclassification risk if the job looks like a normal employee role | Higher misclassification risk if the contractor behaves like staff on a roster |
| Best fit | Counter service, packing, baking support, routine shifts | Specialist work, short-term projects, overflow support with clear deliverables |

## Practical Decision Framework

### Choose a **part-time employee** if:
- You need someone on **set shifts** each week.
- The role is part of the bakery’s normal operations.
- You want to **direct tasks closely** and maintain consistent service.
- You expect ongoing supervision, training, and integration into the team.

### Choose a **contractor** if:
- The work is **clearly independent** and not tightly supervised.
- You need **specialized help** for a defined task or outcome.
- You want flexibility to engage someone without building a regular roster.
- The person brings their own methods, tools, and business setup.

## Simple Rule of Thumb for This Bakery

- If the person will be **working like staff** — serving customers, helping production, following your roster, taking day-to-day direction — treat it as a **part-time employee**.
- If the person will be **running an independent service** — for example, a one-off marketing project, bookkeeping support, or a defined catering job — a **contractor** may be a better fit.

For a **20-hour/week, 6-month bakery role**, the pattern sounds more like **part-time employment** than contracting, especially if the work is regular and operational.
